annotations: The evolutionary rate of clade A and clade B strains, respectively, across all the genes were 8.0 and 7.6 × 10⁻⁴ substitutions site⁻¹ year⁻¹ for GPC, 9.9 and 10.2 × 10⁻⁴ for NP, 7.8 and 8.1 × 10⁻⁴ for L, and 14.5 and 13.5 × 10⁻⁴ for the Z gene (Table 2).

The article estimates that human-to-human transmission is responsible for 20% of LASV transmissions (from the Introduction section: "Human-to-human transmission is also one of the routes of transmission, especially in hospital settings, and this has been estimated to be responsible for 20% of LASV transmissions...")
Generation time (time between primary and secondary cases) was derived empirically from nosocomial and extra‑nosocomial outbreaks and presented in Figs. 3.C, 3.D and S2 Text.
The analyses show that almost 20% of the cases at KGH are secondary cases arising from human-to-human transmission.

The article reports estimates of effective reproduction number, e.g., "we found only 5% of human cases result in an effective reproduction number (i.e. the average number of secondary cases per infectious case) w1, with a maximum value up to 12."

The article estimates seroprevalence of multiple arthropod-borne and hemorrhagic fever viruses in Sierra Leone. In Table 2, the authors report seroprevalence percentages such as: Dengue virus 11/253 (4.3%), West Nile virus 7/253 (2.8%), Yellow fever 5/201 (2.5%), Rift Valley fever 5/253 (2.0%), Chikungunya 10/253 (4.0%), Ebola virus 19/220 (8.6%), and Marburg virus 8/220 (3.6%). These represent seroprevalence estimates from actual patient samples tested at the Kenema Government Hospital Lassa Diagnostic Laboratory.
